q: A phlebotomist enters an outpatient drawing station and calls the next name on the list. Which set of identifiers meets the two-identifier requirement?
choices: Room number and bed assignment
Physical appearance and the name on the requisition
Full name and date of birth stated by the patient
The name the patient answers to when called from the waiting room
why: Two independent identifiers such as full name and date of birth, stated by the patient and matched to the requisition, are required. Calling a name and accepting a nod is not acceptable because patients with hearing loss or similar names commonly answer to the wrong name.

q: An unconscious trauma patient arrives in the emergency department with no identification. How should the phlebotomist identify the patient before the draw?
choices: Use the temporary identification number assigned by the facility and attached to the patient
Wait until a family member arrives to give a name
Label the tubes as unknown male and add a name later
Ask the paramedic to state a name from the scene
why: Facilities assign a temporary or John or Jane Doe number that is banded to the patient and used on the requisition and labels. Waiting for family delays emergent testing and is not required once the temporary number exists.

q: A phlebotomist is drawing an inpatient. The armband is not on the patient but is taped to the bedside table. What is the correct action?
choices: Use the armband on the table since it is the correct patient
Ask the patient to hold the band while identifying
Draw the patient and ask nursing to reband afterward
Have the nurse reband the patient before the draw
why: An inpatient armband is only valid while attached to the patient; a loose band must be replaced by nursing before collection. Using the band from the table is a common identification error because it cannot be tied to the person in the bed.

q: Which element is NOT required on a laboratory requisition?
choices: Ordering provider name
Phlebotomist home address
Tests requested
Patient full name and date of birth
why: Requisitions require patient identifiers, ordering provider, tests requested, date and time, and any special instructions. The collector's personal address is never part of the requisition, although the collector's initials or ID go on the tube label.

q: A phlebotomist notices that a basic metabolic panel appears twice on the same patient for the same collection time. What should be done?
choices: Contact the nursing unit or laboratory to verify whether the duplicate order is intended before collecting
Draw two separate sets to satisfy both orders
Cancel one order independently and collect once
Collect once and discard the second requisition
why: Duplicate orders are verified with the unit or laboratory so the patient is not drawn twice unnecessarily. The phlebotomist does not have the authority to cancel a physician order on their own.

q: Which statement best reflects proper introduction technique at the bedside?
choices: Enter quietly and begin assembling supplies without speaking
Introduce yourself only if the patient asks who you are
State your name, your department, and explain that you are there to collect a blood sample
Tell the patient the draw will not hurt at all
why: A proper introduction includes the collector's name, department, and purpose of the visit, which reduces anxiety and supports consent. Promising that it will not hurt is false reassurance and destroys trust when the needle is inserted.

q: A competent adult extends her arm and rolls up her sleeve after the phlebotomist explains the venipuncture. This is an example of which type of consent?
choices: Informed consent
Implied consent
Expressed written consent
Surrogate consent
why: Implied consent is demonstrated by the patient's cooperative actions rather than words. Informed consent involves a documented discussion of risks, benefits, and alternatives and is typically required for more invasive procedures.

q: An alert inpatient states that he does not want his blood drawn. What should the phlebotomist do?
choices: Draw the sample because the physician ordered it
Ask a family member to convince the patient
Return in one hour and attempt the draw without asking
Stop, document the refusal, and notify the nurse or ordering provider
why: A competent patient has the right to refuse; proceeding anyway could constitute battery. The refusal must be documented and communicated so the care team can follow up rather than simply being retried without discussion.

q: Which approach is most appropriate when preparing to draw blood from a 4-year-old child?
choices: Tell the child the needle will not be used
Explain the full procedure 30 minutes in advance to prepare the child
Use simple honest language, keep the explanation brief, and allow a parent to help comfort the child
Ask the parent to restrain the child alone in the hallway
why: Short, honest, age-appropriate explanations with a parent providing comfort work best for preschoolers. Long advance explanations increase anticipatory anxiety in young children.

q: An elderly patient with thin, fragile skin and poor vein elasticity is scheduled for a routine draw. Which modification is most appropriate?
choices: Apply the tourniquet loosely or use a blood pressure cuff at low pressure and anchor the vein carefully
Apply the tourniquet very tightly to distend the vein
Use a 16 gauge needle to speed collection
Slap the antecubital area briskly to raise the vein
why: Fragile skin and veins call for reduced tourniquet pressure and careful anchoring to prevent bruising and vein rolling. A tight tourniquet increases the risk of skin tears and hematoma in geriatric patients.

q: A patient tells the phlebotomist that she fainted during her last blood draw. What is the best preparation step?
choices: Draw the blood quickly while the patient stands
Have the patient hold her breath during the draw
Withhold the draw until a physician is present
Place the patient in a supine or reclined position before beginning
why: A history of syncope calls for reclining the patient so a faint does not result in a fall injury. Drawing a fainting-prone patient while standing is the highest risk position.

q: A patient scheduled for a lipid panel asks how long she must fast. What is the standard instruction?
choices: 4 to 6 hours with no water
9 to 12 hours with water permitted
2 hours with clear liquids permitted
24 hours with nothing by mouth
why: Lipid panels traditionally require a 9 to 12 hour fast, and water is allowed and encouraged to prevent dehydration. Withholding water is incorrect because dehydration hemoconcentrates the specimen.

q: A fasting blood glucose is ordered. Which fasting interval is standard?
choices: 8 to 10 hours
1 to 2 hours
16 to 20 hours
No fasting is needed
why: Fasting blood glucose generally requires 8 to 10 hours without food. Prolonged fasting beyond about 12 hours is not recommended because it can alter results and stress the patient.

q: Which best defines the basal state?
choices: Any time the patient has not eaten for 4 hours
The condition immediately after moderate exercise
The resting metabolic state early in the morning after about 12 hours of fasting and no strenuous activity
The state of the patient during an active infection
why: Basal state refers to a resting, fasting condition roughly 12 hours after the last intake, typically obtained in the early morning before activity. A short 4-hour fast does not produce basal conditions.

q: A patient smoked a cigarette 10 minutes before arriving for a draw. Which effect is most likely?
choices: Decreased hemoglobin
Elevated white blood cell count and cortisol
Decreased glucose
No measurable effect on any analyte
why: Smoking transiently raises WBC count, cortisol, and glucose among other analytes. It does not lower hemoglobin; chronic smoking actually tends to raise hemoglobin and hematocrit.

q: A patient reports finishing an intense workout 20 minutes ago. Which action is most appropriate?
choices: Proceed with the draw with no comment
Cancel the test permanently
Have the patient drink a sports beverage first
Allow the patient to rest and note the recent exercise for the laboratory
why: Strenuous exercise elevates creatine kinase, lactate, and potassium, so rest before collection and documentation of the activity are appropriate. Giving a sports beverage would further alter glucose and electrolytes.

q: A serum cortisol is ordered and no collection time is specified. Why does timing matter?
choices: Cortisol is unaffected by time of day
Cortisol is highest at midnight
Cortisol shows diurnal variation and peaks in the early morning, around 0800
Cortisol can only be drawn while fasting
why: Cortisol follows a diurnal rhythm with a peak around 0800 and a trough late in the evening, so collection time must be recorded. Midnight represents the low point, not the peak.

q: Which analyte also demonstrates diurnal variation, typically running higher in the morning?
choices: Serum iron
Serum albumin
Total protein
Chloride
why: Serum iron is highest in the morning and drops later in the day, so timed collection matters. Albumin and total protein vary mainly with posture and hydration rather than a daily rhythm.

q: A trough level for vancomycin should be collected at which time?
choices: 30 minutes after the infusion ends
Immediately before the next scheduled dose
Midway between two doses
Any time convenient for the unit
why: A trough reflects the lowest concentration and is drawn immediately before the next dose. A sample taken 30 minutes after an infusion would approximate a peak, not a trough.

q: A peak drug level is ordered for an intramuscular antibiotic. When is it generally drawn?
choices: Immediately before the dose is given
12 hours after the dose
At the same time as the trough
About 30 minutes to 1 hour after administration, per protocol
why: Peak levels are collected after absorption is complete, commonly about 30 to 60 minutes after an IM dose depending on the drug and facility protocol. Drawing before the dose yields a trough.

q: Which instruction is correct for a patient scheduled for a 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test?
choices: Fast 8 to 12 hours beforehand, then drink the entire glucose solution within 5 minutes
Eat a low carbohydrate breakfast before arriving
Sip the glucose solution slowly over 1 hour
Chew gum during the test to reduce nausea
why: The GTT requires a fast of 8 to 12 hours and the glucose load is consumed within about 5 minutes, with timing started at the last swallow. Gum stimulates digestion and can alter glucose results.

q: During a glucose tolerance test the patient vomits 15 minutes after drinking the solution. What should the phlebotomist do?
choices: Give a second dose of glucose and restart
Continue and note the vomiting on the final tube only
Notify the provider or laboratory because the test may need to be rescheduled
Shorten the test to 1 hour
why: Vomiting invalidates the glucose load, so the provider or laboratory decides whether to stop and reschedule. The phlebotomist cannot redose the patient on their own authority.

q: A patient scheduled for a fasting lipid panel admits to drinking coffee with cream 2 hours ago. What is the best action?
choices: Proceed and say nothing
Wait 30 minutes and then draw
Have the patient drink water and draw immediately
Notify the provider or laboratory and reschedule or note the nonfasting status
why: Coffee with cream breaks the fast and affects triglycerides, so the nonfasting status must be reported and the draw rescheduled or flagged. Waiting 30 minutes does not restore a fasting state.

q: Which beverage is generally permitted during a fast?
choices: Black coffee
Plain water
Unsweetened tea
Diet soda
why: Only plain water is permitted during a fast, and it helps prevent hemoconcentration. Black coffee is not allowed because caffeine alters several analytes even without calories.

q: A visibly anxious adult patient states he has a strong fear of needles. Which action is best?
choices: Tell him to stop worrying because it is quick
Show him the needle to prove it is small
Speak calmly, recline him, and use distraction while working efficiently
Have him stand so he can leave quickly if needed
why: Calm communication, a reclined position, and distraction lower the risk of a vasovagal response in needle-phobic patients. Displaying the needle typically escalates anxiety.

q: A seated patient becomes pale and diaphoretic during a draw. What is the first action?
choices: Remove the tourniquet and needle, then lower the patient's head and apply a cold compress
Finish filling the remaining tubes quickly
Leave the patient to get help
Give the patient juice immediately while upright
why: The draw must be terminated immediately and the patient protected from a fall, with the head lowered and a cold compress applied. Leaving a syncopal patient unattended risks an unwitnessed fall injury.

q: A patient had a left-sided mastectomy with lymph node removal 3 months ago. Which arm should be used?
choices: Left arm, because the surgery is healed
Right arm, avoiding the side of the mastectomy
Either arm at the phlebotomist's discretion
Neither arm; only a finger stick is allowed
why: Draws are avoided on the side of a mastectomy with lymph node dissection because of lymphostasis and infection risk, so the unaffected side is used. A 3-month interval does not remove the restriction; provider approval is required for the affected side.

q: A patient has an IV running in the left forearm and no accessible veins in the right arm. What is the preferred approach?
choices: Draw directly above the running IV
Draw from the IV line without stopping the infusion
Draw from the IV site itself
Draw below the IV after the nurse has stopped the infusion for 2 minutes, and document it
why: If no alternative site exists, collection is made distal to the site after the infusion is stopped for about 2 minutes, with a discard volume and documentation. Drawing above a running IV contaminates the specimen with infusing fluid.

q: The only accessible antecubital area shows a large purple hematoma. What should the phlebotomist do?
choices: Select a different vein distal to the hematoma or use the other arm
Draw through the hematoma since the vein is visible
Massage the hematoma to disperse it, then draw
Apply the tourniquet directly over the hematoma
why: Blood drawn through a hematoma is contaminated with hemolyzed extravascular blood and gives erroneous results, so another site is chosen. Massaging a hematoma causes pain and further tissue damage.

q: Why should venipuncture be avoided in an edematous arm?
choices: Edema makes the skin too tough to penetrate
Edema increases clotting factors in the sample
Excess tissue fluid alters test results and the site heals poorly
Edema makes veins bleed excessively
why: Edematous tissue contains excess interstitial fluid that dilutes and contaminates the specimen, and the compromised tissue heals poorly. Edema does not raise clotting factors in the drawn sample.

q: A patient has extensive scarring from burns across both antecubital areas. Which action is most appropriate?
choices: Draw through the scar tissue using a larger gauge needle
Select an alternative site such as a hand vein away from the scarred and burned tissue
Apply heat to the scars to soften them
Refuse to collect the sample
why: Scarred and burned skin is difficult to penetrate, painful, and prone to infection, so an unaffected site such as a hand vein is used. Refusing to collect is unnecessary when alternative sites exist.

q: A patient has a cast on the right arm and a dialysis fistula in the left forearm. What should the phlebotomist do?
choices: Draw from the fistula since it has excellent flow
Draw from the arm with the cast above the cast edge
Use a capillary stick on a toe
Look for an acceptable vein such as a hand vein on the fistula arm only with provider approval, or consult the nurse
why: A fistula or graft is never used or compressed by a phlebotomist, and a casted limb is avoided, so the nurse or provider must direct the alternative. Puncturing a fistula risks clotting and loss of the access.

q: A patient requests the draw be taken through a large forearm tattoo. What is the best response?
choices: Proceed because tattoo ink does not affect specimens
Use the tattoo only if it is older than 1 year
Choose a vein outside the tattooed area whenever possible
Cleanse the tattoo twice and proceed
why: Tattooed skin may be more prone to infection, can obscure vein visualization, and dye may interfere, so an untattooed site is preferred. Extra cleansing does not resolve these issues.

q: The intended site has active dermatitis with open, weeping skin. What is the correct action?
choices: Select a different site away from the affected skin
Cleanse with extra alcohol and proceed
Cover the rash with gauze and puncture through it
Use povidone-iodine instead of alcohol and proceed
why: Compromised skin should not be punctured because of infection risk to both patient and collector, so another site is chosen. Changing the antiseptic does not make damaged skin an acceptable puncture site.

q: Where should a tourniquet be applied, and for how long?
choices: Directly over the antecubital fossa for 3 minutes
6 to 8 inches above the site for 2 minutes
At the wrist for 1 minute
3 to 4 inches above the intended site for no more than 1 minute
why: Standard practice is 3 to 4 inches proximal to the site with a maximum of 1 minute to avoid hemoconcentration. Leaving it on 2 to 3 minutes falsely elevates analytes such as potassium and total protein.

q: A phlebotomist has spent 90 seconds locating a vein with the tourniquet on. What should be done?
choices: Continue searching since the vein is almost found
Release the tourniquet, wait 2 minutes, then reapply
Tighten the tourniquet to improve filling
Have the patient pump the fist vigorously
why: If the tourniquet has been on longer than 1 minute it is released and reapplied after about 2 minutes to let circulation normalize. Vigorous fist pumping falsely raises potassium.

q: Which characteristic best identifies a suitable vein on palpation?
choices: Bouncy and resilient with a defined path
Hard and cordlike
Pulsating with each heartbeat
Flat and nonpalpable but clearly visible
why: A good vein feels bouncy and resilient and can be traced. A pulsating vessel is an artery and a hard cordlike vessel is likely sclerosed or thrombosed.

q: In the H-shaped antecubital vein pattern, which vein is the first choice?
choices: Basilic vein
Cephalic vein
Median cubital vein
Brachial vein
why: The median cubital vein is the first choice because it is large, well anchored, and farthest from the brachial artery and median nerve. The basilic vein is a last resort for exactly the opposite reasons.

q: In the M-shaped antecubital pattern, which vein is generally selected first?
choices: Median basilic vein
Median cephalic vein
Basilic vein
Accessory cephalic vein
why: In the M pattern the median cephalic, on the lateral or thumb side, is the preferred first choice. The median basilic lies medially near the brachial artery and median nerve and is chosen last.

q: Why is the basilic vein the last choice for venipuncture?
choices: It is too superficial to enter
It collapses under any tourniquet pressure
It is always thrombosed
It lies close to the brachial artery and median nerve
why: The basilic vein's proximity to the brachial artery and median nerve makes accidental arterial puncture and nerve injury more likely. It is not inherently thrombosed or too superficial.

q: A phlebotomist decides to use a dorsal hand vein. Which preparation change is appropriate?
choices: Use a 16 gauge needle and a large evacuated tube
Apply the tourniquet at the elbow only
Use a winged infusion set with a smaller gauge needle and anchor the vein firmly
Insert at a 45 degree angle
why: Hand veins are small and mobile, so a winged set with a 23 gauge needle and firm anchoring is standard. A large bore needle with high vacuum is likely to collapse the vein.

q: A patient's veins are difficult to locate. Which warming technique is appropriate?
choices: Apply a warm compress at about 42 degrees Celsius for 3 to 5 minutes
Immerse the arm in hot water for 15 minutes
Use a heating pad on the highest setting for 10 minutes
Rub the site briskly with alcohol until warm
why: Warming at approximately 42 degrees Celsius for 3 to 5 minutes increases blood flow safely. Higher temperatures or prolonged application risk burns, especially in infants and the elderly.

q: Why should a phlebotomist avoid slapping the antecubital area to raise a vein?
choices: It leaves a visible mark that confuses site selection
It causes hemolysis and petechiae and is painful and unprofessional
It permanently damages the median nerve
It causes arterial spasm and loss of pulse
why: Slapping bruises tissue, can hemolyze blood, and is unprofessional; gentle massage upward from the wrist is the alternative. It does not cause permanent nerve damage or loss of pulse.

q: Which statement about vigorous fist pumping before a draw is correct?
choices: It is required to fill the vein adequately
It has no effect on any laboratory value
It is recommended for all chemistry draws
It should be avoided because it falsely elevates potassium and ionized calcium
why: Muscle activity releases potassium from cells and alters ionized calcium and lactate, so the patient makes a fist without pumping. A single closed fist is acceptable; repeated pumping is not.

q: What is the correct technique for cleansing a routine venipuncture site?
choices: Cleanse with 70% isopropyl alcohol in concentric circles or a back-and-forth motion and allow it to air dry for 30 seconds
Cleanse with alcohol and blot dry with gauze immediately
Cleanse with sterile water and dry with gauze
Cleanse with alcohol and fan the site dry with your hand
why: 70% isopropyl alcohol must be allowed to air dry about 30 seconds to be effective and to prevent stinging and specimen hemolysis. Blotting or fanning recontaminates the site and cuts the contact time short.

q: A phlebotomist re-palpates the cleansed site immediately before inserting the needle. What must be done?
choices: Nothing, the glove keeps the site sterile
Wipe the glove with alcohol only
Cleanse the site again with 70% alcohol and allow it to dry
Insert the needle quickly to limit contamination
why: Touching the prepared site recontaminates it, so it must be recleansed and allowed to dry. Gloves are not sterile, so glove contact does not preserve the prepared site.

q: Which antiseptic is appropriate for skin preparation before collecting blood cultures on an adult?
choices: 70% isopropyl alcohol alone
Chlorhexidine gluconate
Sterile saline
Hydrogen peroxide
why: Chlorhexidine gluconate is the standard blood culture skin prep for adults and patients over 2 months. Alcohol alone does not provide sufficient residual antisepsis to prevent contaminated cultures.

q: Blood cultures are ordered on a 6-week-old infant. Which antiseptic is generally preferred?
choices: Chlorhexidine gluconate
Benzalkonium chloride
Povidone-iodine
Alcohol only, followed by drying
why: Povidone-iodine is commonly used for infants under 2 months because chlorhexidine is not recommended for that age group. Alcohol alone remains inadequate for culture collection at any age.

q: A blood alcohol level is ordered for a legal case. Which site prep is correct?
choices: 70% isopropyl alcohol
Ethyl alcohol swab
Tincture of iodine
A nonalcohol antiseptic such as benzalkonium chloride or soap and water
why: Alcohol-based antiseptics can contaminate the specimen and are challenged in court, so a nonalcohol antiseptic is required. Isopropyl alcohol is not acceptable even though it is not the alcohol being measured.

q: While preparing the tray, the phlebotomist notices that a box of evacuated tubes expired last month. What should be done?
choices: Remove the expired tubes from service and obtain unexpired tubes
Use them only for chemistry tests
Use them if the vacuum still draws blood
Use them and note the expiration on the requisition
why: Expired tubes may have lost vacuum and degraded additives, producing inaccurate results, so they are removed from use. Successfully drawing blood does not prove that the additive is still effective.

q: Which needle gauge is most appropriate for a routine adult antecubital venipuncture with an evacuated tube system?
choices: 16 gauge
21 or 22 gauge
25 gauge
18 gauge
why: A 21 gauge is the standard multisample needle, with 22 gauge used for smaller veins. A 25 gauge is used for capillary or very small veins and increases hemolysis risk with vacuum draws.

q: A patient speaks only Spanish and the phlebotomist speaks only English. What is the best action before the draw?
choices: Use hand gestures and proceed
Ask the patient's 8-year-old child to interpret
Obtain a qualified interpreter or facility language service before explaining the procedure
Skip the explanation since the procedure is routine
why: A qualified interpreter or language line ensures accurate explanation and valid consent. Using a minor child as an interpreter is not acceptable practice.

q: A patient who is hard of hearing is scheduled for a draw. Which technique is most effective?
choices: Face the patient, speak clearly at a moderate pace, and confirm understanding
Shout from the doorway
Speak only to the accompanying family member
Write nothing and rely on gestures alone
why: Facing the patient at a moderate pace supports lip reading and comprehension, and understanding is confirmed. Shouting distorts speech and bypassing the patient to address family is disrespectful and risks identification errors.

q: Before entering an airborne isolation room to draw blood, what should the phlebotomist do?
choices: Bring the entire phlebotomy tray into the room for convenience
Put on gloves only
Enter first and don PPE at the bedside
Take only the needed supplies and don the required PPE, including a fit-tested respirator, before entering
why: Only necessary supplies enter an isolation room, and all required PPE including an N95 respirator is donned before entry. Bringing the full tray in risks contaminating equipment used on other patients.

q: Which information should be confirmed and documented before the needle is inserted?
choices: The patient's insurance carrier
Patient identification, test orders, fasting status, and any site restrictions or allergies
The results of the previous week's tests
The patient's next scheduled appointment
why: Identification, orders, fasting status, and site or allergy restrictions such as latex must be verified before the puncture. Insurance and appointment details are clerical and do not affect specimen integrity or patient safety.
